reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / movement disorder literature
clinicalPearls: Rhythmic involuntary movement of the soft palate with no identifiable structural brain lesion
The characteristic complaint is an objective clicking tinnitus that the examiner may also hear, produced by rhythmic opening of the Eustachian tube
Contraction of the tensor veli palatini muscle is responsible for the ear click
It typically stops during sleep, unlike the symptomatic form which often persists
MRI is normal, in contrast to symptomatic palatal tremor with hypertrophic olivary degeneration
A proportion of cases are functional, so positive functional signs should be sought
reference.pathophysiology: Essential palatal tremor is characterised by rhythmic contraction of the tensor veli palatini, which rhythmically opens the Eustachian tube and generates an audible click perceived as objective tinnitus. Unlike symptomatic palatal tremor, there is no lesion in the Guillain-Mollaret triangle and no hypertrophic olivary degeneration, and the underlying mechanism is uncertain, with some cases having a functional basis. The absence of a structural substrate and the frequent disappearance during sleep distinguish it from the symptomatic form.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of objective tinnitus (vascular, patulous Eustachian tube)
additionalInvestigations: Direct examination of the soft palate for rhythmic movement
Otological assessment of the clicking tinnitus
MRI of the brainstem to exclude a lesion causing symptomatic tremor
Assessment for functional signs such as distractibility and variability
redFlags: Persistence during sleep or associated pendular nystagmus suggesting the symptomatic form
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign though the click can be distressing; it may remit spontaneously or fluctuate, and various treatments including botulinum toxin to the palatal muscle are used with variable success.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish it from symptomatic palatal tremor by imaging and sleep behaviour
Overlooking middle-ear myoclonus as an alternative cause of objective clicking
Dismissing the objective tinnitus as subjective
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Reassurance and explanation of the benign nature once a structural cause is excluded
Botulinum toxin injection into the tensor and levator veli palatini muscles for troublesome objective clicking tinnitus
Assess for a functional component and offer psychological or behavioural therapy where positive functional signs are present
Exclude symptomatic palatal tremor with brainstem MRI before committing to treatment
Otological and audiological assessment and management of the tinnitus
Coordinate care between neurology and otolaryngology
